title: Cadence, Nvidia Unveil New AI Models To Put EDA On Autopilot
gist: Cadence says 20 to 30 percent of chips under development are being designed with AI agents, and it launched Maestro models fine-tuned on Nvidia Nemotron that claim up to 30 percent higher output quality and up to 5x better token efficiency than general-purpose foundation models. The article uses it as an example of generative AI and HPC converging in industry and science.

insights.claim: Cadence senior VP Paul Cunningham estimates that 20 to 30 percent of chips under development are being designed with the help of AI agents and that the share is growing rapidly.
insights.speaker: Paul Cunningham
insights.so_what: If this is correct, AI-assisted design is already routine in chip development, which affects EDA vendors and chip designers. It is a vendor executive's estimate.
insights.quote: somewhere between 20 and 30 percent of chips under development today are being designed with the help of AI agents
insights.locator: Like a virus, generative AI has invaded

insights.claim: Cadence has released "AI Super Agents" for different design tasks: AuraStack (advanced packaging and PCB layout), ChipStack (SoC design and verification), InnoStack (PHY routing) and ViraStack (analog circuit design).
insights.speaker: Tobias Mann
insights.so_what: Cadence is covering the main design flows with agent products rather than a single tool.
insights.locator: Over the past year or so, the EDA giant

insights.claim: The agent harnesses resemble coding tools such as Claude Code or Codex and orchestrate existing EDA, test and verification tools. The approach works for the same reason as AI code assistants: code either compiles or it doesn't, and Cadence has tests that verify designs work as intended.
insights.speaker: Tobias Mann
insights.so_what: Verifiable output is what makes agents effective, so domains with hard checks such as chip design are adopted first.
insights.quote: Code either compiles or it doesn't.

themes.theme: Domain specialization of models: Maestro and Nemotron

insights.claim: Cadence's early agents used off-the-shelf LLMs with limited exposure to hardware descriptions such as RTL. Their effectiveness depends on how closely the training data matches the inputs and outputs they are given.
insights.speaker: Tobias Mann
insights.so_what: General models hit a ceiling in specialized domains, which creates room for domain-tuned models.
insights.locator: But just like many code assistants

insights.claim: Cunningham argues that powerful out-of-the-box foundation models are a starting point and will not do everything, and that they can still be specialized.
insights.speaker: Paul Cunningham
insights.so_what: This supports the case for vertical post-training and against the view that general models will absorb every domain.
insights.quote: It’s not the case that these amazingly powerful out-of-the-box foundation models are just going to do everything.
insights.locator: Over the past year or so

insights.claim: This week Cadence announced a partnership with Nvidia and launched the Maestro AI model family, fine-tuned on Nvidia's Nemotron models to work with and interpret the output of Cadence's tools.
insights.speaker: Tobias Mann
insights.so_what: Nemotron is being used as a base model by an EDA vendor, which extends Nvidia's reach beyond hardware.
insights.quote: this week Cadence announced a partnership with Nvidia and launched its Maestro AI model family
insights.locator: In a bid for greater specialization

insights.claim: Cadence says early testing of Maestro showed "up to" a 30 percent increase in output quality and "up to" 5x better token efficiency than general-purpose foundation models, meaning the post-trained models are both smarter and cheaper to run. These are vendor claims, and "up to" figures are best-case.
insights.speaker: Tobias Mann
insights.so_what: If the gains hold, specialized models cut inference cost per design, which strengthens vertical AI economics.
insights.quote: "up to" 30 percent increase in output quality and "up to" 5x greater token efficiency

insights.claim: Maestro can be customized with customer data, but Cunningham says that will be offered as a managed service rather than something customers do themselves. The models can be reached by API, run in a secure VPC or run on-prem for customers with the hardware.
insights.speaker: Tobias Mann
insights.so_what: Cadence keeps the fine-tuning work for itself, which protects margins and customer lock-in.
insights.locator: Along with the models, Cadence's Maestro platform

insights.claim: Nvidia has been pushing HPC into a collision course with AI for years. The idea of AI-driven labs is also central to the Department of Energy's Genesis Mission, which has produced a flurry of new large Nvidia-based supercomputers.
insights.speaker: Tobias Mann
insights.so_what: Government science programs are adding to demand for Nvidia systems.
insights.locator: Cadence isn't the only one exploring

insights.claim: Sandia National Labs recently demonstrated AI agents developing and testing hypotheses in a self-driving lab, though without modern agent harnesses or LLMs. With limited public research funding, an AI lab assistant that works after hours is attractive to public researchers.
insights.speaker: Tobias Mann
insights.so_what: Cheap agent labor appeals most to budget-constrained researchers, which could widen adoption in public science.
insights.quote: Given the limited funding afforded public researchers
